title: Optimising Lab Protocols
answer: Optimising lab protocols covers the use of computational methods to improve the design, scheduling and execution of wet lab procedures. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Optimising lab protocols covers the use of computational methods to improve the design, scheduling and execution of wet lab procedures. It sits within laboratory automation and simulation, where the goal is fewer failed runs, less reagent waste and more reproducible results. The work spans protocol representation, resource scheduling, liquid handling and the simulation of a protocol before it is run at the bench.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of scheduling and simulation software, laboratory information management systems and the control software of automated liquid handlers and robotic platforms. Protocols are often encoded in machine readable formats so that a scheduler or a simulator can reason about steps, timings and dependencies. Some groups also use machine learning models trained on historical run data to predict failure points or suggest parameter changes.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners begin by capturing a protocol as an explicit sequence of steps with durations, volumes, equipment and constraints. They then simulate or schedule that sequence to find bottlenecks, conflicts and risky steps before any physical run. Where enough historical data exists, models can be fitted to predict outcomes such as yield or contamination risk, and the protocol is revised and re-simulated. Validation still happens at the bench, because simulation is a guide rather than a substitute for a real run.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on data ownership, instrument vendor terms and the provenance of any model used to alter a protocol. Records of which protocol version was run, on which instrument and with which parameters matter for reproducibility and for any later audit. Where patient samples or regulated assays are involved, additional rules on consent, traceability and data handling apply, and the original research paper should be consulted rather than a summary. This page describes practice only and is not legal, regulatory or medical advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter coupling between simulation and execution, so that a protocol can be adjusted in response to instrument feedback during a run. Standard formats for protocol exchange and richer metadata are likely to make results easier to compare across labs. As models take on more of the scheduling and parameter choice, the open questions are how to keep decisions explainable and how to preserve a clear record of what was actually done.
